Menelaus From Ceva

GeometryTrianglesAlgebra
Game: Move dots on a triangle and watch one straight line cross all three sides; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag a dot with a mouse or finger, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Tick “Show add-ons” for the extra lines, and press Reset to start over.
Look for the math

Two famous triangle facts look quite different: one is about three lines through a single point, the other about three dots on a single line. This picture shows why each one follows from the other.

Three cevians, one point

In Ceva's theorem, the lines AD, BE and CF go from the corners to the opposite sides. They meet at one point exactly when

AF/FB × BD/DC × CE/EA = 1

Here each quotient compares two pieces of the same side. The segments are directed: travelling along a side in one chosen direction, a piece against that direction counts as negative.

Three dots, one line

In Menelaus' theorem, F on AB, D on BC and E on AC are collinear exactly when

AF/BF × BD/CD × CE/AE = 1

Only the order of the letters changed: FB became BF, and so on. Reversing all three segments flips the sign three times, which is why the sign check at the end matters. The logic test checks this both ways over a grid of side fractions: the product is 1 precisely when the three dots are on one straight line.

Six applications of Ceva

Let X be where BE meets AD, Y where AD meets CF, and Z where BE meets CF. Tick “Show add-ons” to see them. Applying Ceva in the triangles ABE, ACD, BCF, BDE, ADF and CEF gives six equations whose left sides multiply together. After cancelling, what is left is

(AF/BF × BD/CD × CE/AE)2 = 1

The check script transcribes those six identities straight from the page and confirms each equals 1 in hundreds of configurations, and that their product is the square above.

Choosing the positive square root

A straight line crossing a triangle's sides cannot cut all three between their endpoints: it misses either one side or all three, meeting their extensions instead. Counting the signs of the three quotients then leaves an even number of negative terms, so the product in the square equation is positive, not negative. Hence Menelaus' product is +1. That is Ceva implying Menelaus, the converse of the proof already given on the original page.

One quirk of the Java applet is kept: dragging a side dot rebuilds the next dot in the cycle E → D → F → E, and dragging a corner only refreshes one dot before rebuilding another. The positions therefore follow the applet's own update order, not a fresh construction from scratch.

Try dragging E past the corner A: watch the status line stay at 1 even though the dot has left the side of the triangle.
